findings.text: The opening explains plainly what Athena is, what a study is, and why this page is about a different project. A newcomer can say what they are looking at within three short paragraphs.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository." and "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: The lede names Athena's selling points: one model checks another, and costs are recorded. Nothing on the page shows either one: no request that produced the study, no checker verdict, no cost. A newcomer weighing Athena has to take these points on trust.
findings.source: "It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The next step is clear and is also linked from the header. It gives no prerequisites, such as a Rust toolchain, model access or API keys, so the reader must go to the repository before the commands are any use.
findings.source: Heading "Next steps": "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page defines its key terms (captain, yolo, green, red) before using them, and gives a three-part overview, which makes a dense topic easier to enter. Some words still appear before any definition outside the Glossary, for example "spawn exits 75" and "Teardown returns the worktree" in "One piece of work, start to finish".

Most of the page is a detailed state machine with claim citations after almost every sentence. That suits someone checking firstmate's internals. For a newcomer who came to learn about Athena, it is long and repetitive: the same yolo/red/place rules come back in Start here, the cards, the design choices and the Glossary.
findings.source: Heading "Transitions" (t1–t11 cards) and "Claims and sources" (44 claims)

findings.text: The page is honest about its limits: it says nothing was run, and it pins the commit it read. This helps a reader judge how far to trust the claims.
findings.source: Heading "Limits of this study": "This study read the pinned tree only... no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: This closing note points to a folder without linking it or saying which repository it is in, so a newcomer cannot follow it.
findings.source: Heading "About this page": "is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
